evidence.claim: A former forest motorway follows Alabama’s highest range to Adams Gap
evidence.quote: Running the crest of the Talladega Mountains, Alabama's highest range, SR 281 was originally an unpaved forest route known as Skyway Motorway prior to the reconstruction into a paved scenic highway.

evidence.claim: to Adams Gap
evidence.quote: end where the pavement ends at Adams Gap and Forest Service Road 600.

evidence.claim: Talladega Scenic Drive follows the crest of Alabama’s highest mountain range on State Route 281.
evidence.quote: Running the crest of the Talladega Mountains, Alabama's highest range

evidence.claim: Talladega Scenic Drive follows the crest of Alabama’s highest mountain range on State Route 281.
evidence.quote: State Route 281 in Alabama, also known as SR 281 and as Talladega Scenic Drive

evidence.claim: The Forest Service presents the drive as 29 miles of mountain and national-forest views, winding along the southern Appalachians.
evidence.quote: The beautiful drive has 29 miles for exploring the Talladega National Forest by automobile. It winds along the backbone of the southern Appalachian mountains and offers spectacular views of the Talladega National Forest.

evidence.claim: Cheaha State Park provides access to the state’s highest natural point.
evidence.quote: Cheaha Mountain , often called Mount Cheaha, is the highest natural point in the U.S. state of Alabama. It is located a few miles northwest of the town of Delta in Cheaha State Park

evidence.claim: The mountain’s stone observation tower looks south across second-growth woodland into Cheaha Wilderness.
evidence.quote: From the stone tower on the summit of Cheaha Mountain, Alabama's highest point at 2,407 feet (734 m), a dense second-growth woodland stretches south across Cheaha State Park and into Cheaha Wilderness.

evidence.claim: Before the pavement, this was the Skyway Motorway, an unpaved forest route.
evidence.quote: SR 281 was originally an unpaved forest route known as Skyway Motorway prior to the reconstruction into a paved scenic highway.

evidence.claim: The scenic drive initially carried the numbers SR 49 and SR 49 Spur.
evidence.quote: When first built, the Talladega Scenic Drive was known as SR 49 and SR 49 Spur.

evidence.claim: The earlier spur climbed to Cheaha Mountain, then continued west toward Talladega as a narrow county road.
evidence.quote: SR 49 Spur extended from where SR 49 ends today to Cheaha Mountain where it continued from there west to Talladega as a narrow county road.

evidence.claim: In the early 1990s, the spur was extended south along the mountains’ western side to a fork of forest roads.
evidence.quote: In the early 1990s, SR 49 Spur was extended south along the western side of the Talladega Mountains, ending at a remote location in the national forest at the fork of two forest roads

evidence.claim: After that work, the spur and the section of SR 49 north of it became SR 281.
evidence.quote: When work was completed on this extension, SR 49 was truncated south of the Spur and both SR 49 north of the spur and the spur itself were both designated as SR 281.

evidence.claim: Start west of Heflin at US 78 and follow SR 281 toward Cheaha.
evidence.quote: The drive starts at the intersection of US 78 and SR 281, just west of Heflin. Simply follow SR 281 through the Talladega National Forest and Cheaha Wilderness

evidence.claim: The road crosses US 431 and I-20 on overpasses without interchanges.
evidence.quote: SR 281 does cross both US 431 and I-20 via overpasses, but does not intersect either of them.

evidence.claim: At Cheaha, Bunker Tower and Bald Rock offer overlooks.
evidence.quote: Scenic overlooks: Cheaha Mountain is topped with Bunker Tower, a stone building with an observation deck on top. A wheelchair-accessible wooden walkway on the Bald Rock Trail provides another overlook of the surrounding region.

evidence.claim: Cheaha Wilderness lies within Talladega National Forest, beside the state park; Congress designated it in 1983 and expanded it in 1988.
evidence.quote: The 7,245-acre (2,932 ha) Cheaha Wilderness lies next to Cheaha State Park, near the Talladega Mountains in Alabama, United States. It lies within the Talladega National Forest and is administrated by the US Forest Service. Congress designated the area on January 3, 1983 and expanded it in 1988.

evidence.claim: Continue south toward Adams Gap, where the scenic drive’s pavement ends at Forest Service Road 600.
evidence.quote: end where the pavement ends at Adams Gap and Forest Service Road 600.

evidence.claim: Alabama’s highest natural point is marked by a USGS benchmark in front of Bunker Tower.
evidence.quote: The highest point is marked with a USGS benchmark in front of Bunker Tower

evidence.claim: The Civilian Conservation Corps completed this native rubble-stone observation tower in 1934.
evidence.quote: Bunker Tower is a native rubble stone building serving as an observation tower on Cheaha Mountain

evidence.claim: The Civilian Conservation Corps completed this native rubble-stone observation tower in 1934.
evidence.quote: The tower, built in a rustic architectural style, was completed in 1934 by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.claim: Its first-floor wings originally held park offices and a gift shop.
evidence.quote: Park offices and a gift shop originally occupied the first floor wings connected to either side of the tower.

evidence.claim: The CCC’s work extended across the park: crews created Cheaha Lake and built stone cabins, pavilions and hiking trails between 1933 and 1939.
evidence.quote: From 1933 to 1939, the Civilian Conservation Corps was active in the park creating Cheaha Lake and building numerous structures including a stone bathhouse, eleven stone cabins, two stone pavilions, Bunker Tower, the Bald Rock Group Lodge, and several hiking trails.

evidence.claim: From the summit tower, second-growth woodland extends south into Cheaha Wilderness.
evidence.quote: From the stone tower on the summit of Cheaha Mountain, Alabama's highest point at 2,407 feet (734 m), a dense second-growth woodland stretches south across Cheaha State Park and into Cheaha Wilderness.

evidence.claim: A tall Alabama Public Television transmitter stands immediately beside the stone tower, another landmark among the trees at the summit.
evidence.quote: The tower is immediately adjacent to a tall Alabama Public Television WCIQ transmitter tower which aids as a landmark among the trees and foliage atop Mount Cheaha.

evidence.claim: A wooden walkway on the Bald Rock Trail leads to an overlook of the surrounding region.
evidence.quote: A wheelchair-accessible wooden walkway on the Bald Rock Trail provides another overlook of the surrounding region.

evidence.claim: On January 4, 1944, a P-38 Lightning flying from Dallas to Atlanta crashed into Bald Rock.
evidence.quote: On January 4, 1944, a P-38 Lightning warplane, piloted by 2nd Lieutenant Chester R. Gunkel of Milwaukee, Wisconsin, was flying from Love Field, Dallas, Texas, to Atlanta, Georgia, and crashed into Bald Rock.

evidence.claim: Its pilot was 2nd Lieutenant Chester R. Gunkel of Milwaukee.
evidence.quote: piloted by 2nd Lieutenant Chester R. Gunkel of Milwaukee, Wisconsin

evidence.claim: A machine gun recovered from the crash site was donated to the park museum in 2023.
evidence.quote: A machine gun was recovered from the crash site and was subsequently donated to the park museum in 2023.

evidence.claim: At Adams Gap, the pavement ends at Forest Service Road 600.
evidence.quote: end where the pavement ends at Adams Gap and Forest Service Road 600.

evidence.claim: The southern highway extension reached a fork of two forest roads in the early 1990s; one belonged to the old Skyway Motorway.
evidence.quote: In the early 1990s, SR 49 Spur was extended south along the western side of the Talladega Mountains, ending at a remote location in the national forest at the fork of two forest roads, one which was part of the old Skyway Motorway.

evidence.claim: The route’s unusual mileposts reflect an unfinished measurement: ALDOT uses Mile 500 as a countdown because the highway’s eventual length is unknown.
evidence.quote: ALDOT uses Mile 500 as a "countdown" mile marker, since the eventual length of highway is not known.

evidence.claim: Those high numbers do not establish that a longer road was always planned.
evidence.quote: The assumption that a longer route has always been planned due to the high mileages posted on the mile markers along the route is incorrect.

evidence.claim: The paved scenic drive ends at Adams Gap and Forest Service Road 600.
evidence.quote: end where the pavement ends at Adams Gap and Forest Service Road 600.

flags: Cache does not verify the catalog’s National Scenic Byway, state byway or National Forest Scenic Byway designations. Formal designation omitted pending evidence.
Sources give conflicting summit elevations (2,405, 2,407 and 2,413 feet); numerical elevation omitted. Cheaha park opening dates also differ (1933 versus 1939); omitted.

Bald Rock and Adams Gap entries are shorter because their focused evidence is limited. Bald Rock and the summit are grouped as the Cheaha stop before Adams Gap; cache does not establish their local driving sequence.
North-to-south presentation reverses the strip-map mile direction. Pavement endpoint checked in the saved Forest Service page only.
The cached Forest Service page gives 29 miles, while catalog geometry gives 26.3. Copy attributes the source distance; no drive time is supplied.
